reason: Under the question on a root volume too small for the memory state, the quote states that without enough space hibernation fails and the instance is shut down instead.
The quote states a hibernated instance is recognized by its state reason, which should be Client.UserInitiatedHibernate.
The quote states stop and hibernate are available for EBS-backed instances only and local instance storage is not persisted.
The quote states hibernation must be enabled at launch and is then triggered with StopInstances plus the Hibernate parameter.
The quote states hibernation suits applications with a long bootstrap, pre-warmed instances resume to cut time to service, and memory state is retained across stop and start.

The quote supports only the RAM part (hibernate persists RAM, stop clears it); the claim's second sentence on EBS root and data volumes persisting in both cases comes from the next sentence, which is not quoted.
The quote states hibernated instances are in the Stopped state.

The quote states virtualized High Memory instances are generally recommended and lists the four cases where only metal works: unsupported OS versions, non-virtualized licensing or support, hardware features such as Intel VT-x, custom hypervisor such as ESXi.
The quote recommends the local instance store for temporary data and EBS volumes or backup to S3 for data needing higher durability.
The quote points to Amazon EC2 Pricing for the list of all instances and regional availability.

The quote gives 5 Gbps single-flow and up to 25 Gbps multiflow within a Region, and up to 10 Gbps single-flow for select instances in a placement group; the instance-type condition is the context sentence before it and is kept in the qualifiers.
The quote supports 'typically less than 10 minutes' from RunInstances to the boot sequence; the claim's factors (AMI size, instance count, recent AMI use) come from the next, unquoted sentence.
The quote states limit increases are tied to the Region they were requested for.
The quote states live update and live migration do not require stop or reboot and customers take no action before, during or after.
The quote states a maximum of 27 additional PCI devices for EBS volumes and ENIs on Nitro Hypervisor instances, with the example of 3 extra ENIs leaving up to 24 EBS volumes.
The quote states the Nitro Hypervisor primarily provides CPU and memory isolation and VPC networking and EBS storage are implemented by Nitro Cards.
The quote recommends NVIDIA GPU-based instances for deep learning and AI models that need CUDA, cuDNN or TensorRT.
The quote states all usage in a family, regardless of generation, size or configuration variant, accrues toward the family's total vCPU limit.

The quote supports the private IP staying across stop and start and the public IP lasting until stop, termination or Elastic IP; the claim's opening ('by default an instance gets a private and a public IP') is in the preceding, unquoted sentence.

The quote supports only 'charged once for a given instance even if both are true'; the two conditions the claim names (different AZ, public or Elastic IP) are in the bullet list after the quote, which is not quoted.
The quote states the AZ can be modified, scope changed between AZ and Region both ways, and size changed within the family on Linux/Unix.
The quote states RIs do not apply to Spot or Dedicated Host instances and points to Dedicated Host Reservations.
Answering the question on transferring a Convertible or Standard RI between Regions, the quote says no: an RI's Region is fixed for the term.
The quote states RIs can still be purchased and work alongside Savings Plans, and AWS encourages Savings Plans as RIs expire for the same savings with more flexibility.
The quote states RIs are only transferable per the RI Marketplace requirements and cannot otherwise be transferred.
The quote supports EBS root data persisting independently of the instance lifetime; the claim's consequence (the instance can be stopped and restarted later) is the next, unquoted sentence.
Under the question comparing instance store and EBS for the root device, the quote states the local instance store only persists during the life of the instance.
The quote states Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation and capacity can be reserved with On-Demand Capacity Reservations at lower prices through Savings Plans.
The quote states Spot is available in all public AWS Regions and for nearly all instance families and sizes.

The claim drops a condition from the same answer: on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server a user who stops or terminates the Spot Instance is charged for an entire hour, so 'charged to the nearest second' does not hold for every OS.
The quote states Spot Fleet does not terminate and relaunch running instances and replenishes a terminated Spot Instance based on the allocation strategy.
The quote supports 'subject to the same availability and prices as a single Spot request'; the explicit 'not guaranteed to be fulfilled' rests on the unquoted 'No.' before it.
The quote states hibernated Spot Instances pause and resume around interruptions and that hibernation fits applications depending on session or other data in RAM.
Under the question on paying for a hibernating Spot Instance, the quote states no extra charge beyond EBS storage and other resources and no instance usage fees once hibernated.
The quote states a hibernated instance cannot be resumed directly, EC2 controls the cycle, and it resumes the instance when capacity becomes available.
The quote states that over the last 3 months 92% of Spot interruptions were customers manually terminating after the application completed its work.
The quote states Spot Instances can be requested up to the Spot limit for each Region and new customers might start lower.
The quote lists Linux/UNIX, Windows Server and RHEL as available and Windows Server with SQL Server as not currently available.
The quote states the Spot price in effect at the beginning of each UTC hour is applied to usage for the subsequent hour.
The two quotes state running Spot Instances are exactly the same as On-Demand or Reserved and Spot is best suited for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads.
